problem: Existing open-vocabulary 3D detection/instance segmentation methods (OVIR-3D, Open3DIS, OpenMask3D, OpenScene) need the whole scene point cloud or heavy 3D networks, which is slow and unsuited to online use on assistive robots such as smart wheelchairs.
motivation: A wheelchair user should be able to name any object and have the chair navigate to it, which needs accurate 3D localization of arbitrary categories in real time without pre-mapping or retraining. Recent open-vocabulary 2D detectors and promptable segmenters could provide this if lifted to 3D using depth.
key_idea: Lift a per-frame zero-shot pipeline of open-vocabulary 2D detector, box-prompted SAM-style mask generator and depth back-projection into 3D instance point clouds, and use their axis-aligned 3D boxes as navigation targets, without building a scene point cloud.
insight: The ablation shows the detector is what matters: switching YoloWorld to GroundingDINO roughly doubles mAP (8.5 to 18.3 with MobileSAM), while swapping MobileSAM for RepViT-SAM adds only about 0.4 to 1.3 mAP. The system trades accuracy on large, partly visible objects (which split into fragments across views) for a 2-4x speedup over Open3DIS, and it does well at relaxed IoU (mAP25).
method: 2D open-vocabulary detection: YoloWorld-S or Grounding-DINO Swin-T detects the text-specified classes on the RGB image and returns boxes, scores and labels.
Mask generator: MobileSAM or RepViT-SAM, prompted with each detected box, produces a binary instance mask.
Morphological erosion: a 3x3 structuring element erodes each mask to remove background noise at the edges.
Depth isolation and Z-score filtering: depth is cropped to each eroded mask and pixels whose depth Z-score exceeds tau=2 are removed.
Point-cloud reconstruction: the filtered depth is back-projected with camera intrinsics K and transformed to world coordinates with extrinsics T.

3D box generation: the min/max extents of each object's world-frame points give an axis-aligned 3D box. Same-class instances from different views are merged if IoU>0.8 for evaluation. The boxes serve as attractors for the wheelchair's APF+MPC controller in ROS2.

setting.observation: RGB-D from a single viewpoint at a time (Intel RealSense D455/D435) with known camera intrinsics and extrinsics
setting.action_space: 3D bounding-box targets fed as attractors to an APF + MPC local planner that outputs linear/angular wheelchair velocity
setting.simulator: Replica dataset (offline evaluation of detection); real wheelchair for navigation
setting.privileged: Camera extrinsics/poses on Replica, plus the full merged scene for evaluation; the real-world case study assumes one object per class

numbers.extra: Per-view predictions merged across 200 views per scene with IoU>0.8; 8 Replica scenes

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark is reported. The Replica split is not named in the paper (8 evaluation scenes), so 'val' is a placeholder. The real-wheelchair results are qualitative trajectories only. Running time: 27.76 s/scene (0.13 s/view) and 94.35 s/scene (0.47 s/view) versus Open3DIS at 197.32 s/scene (0.98 s/view).
results: On Replica, the GDino+RepViT-SAM variant reaches mAP 18.7 / mAP50 29.7 / mAP25 37.7, beating the best baseline Open3DIS (3D) at 18.5 / 24.5 / 28.2, with a small margin on mAP and large margins at relaxed IoU. It is 2-4x faster than Open3DIS, and a qualitative wheelchair demo navigates to person, chair and desk targets.
limitations: Performance is bounded by the 2D detector and segmenter, and large objects that are not fully visible in one view are fragmented into several instances.
The real-world demo assumes one object per class and one target, and gives only qualitative trajectories with no quantitative navigation metrics.
Axis-aligned min/max boxes and depth masking produce shadow artifacts, e.g. missing the central chair and table.
